# Pi-hole Setup

## Overview

A Raspberry Pi 3B with a 32 GB card sits behind the router and filters trackers and advertising domains at the resolver, before they ever reach a browser. That is the whole job, and it does it for every device in the house at once, phones and televisions included. The card is small and cheap, which is exactly why I chose it; a full computer would be wasted on this task. What I like most is that the filtering is not per-device. I do not install anything on the televisions, and I do not maintain a list on each laptop. There is one resolver, and everything asks it. The flip side is the risk I have to plan for. When the Pi goes down, the whole house stops resolving names until the fallback kicks in, and a house that cannot resolve anything feels broken in a way that is hard to explain over dinner. So the fallback resolver is not an optional extra, it is part of the design. I keep a second Pi on the shelf with the same image, and I have written down the address and the settings so that swapping it in is a matter of minutes rather than an evening. The card and the Pi together cost less than a single month of the subscriptions I no longer pay for, which is why I find it odd that more people do not run one. It also taught me something about my own house, because the query log showed me devices I did not know were talking to the outside world at all, and a couple of those conversations were ones I decided to stop.

## Setup

I started by flashing the card with the current image and, before even booting the Pi, giving it a static lease on the router. Setting the lease first saves a great deal of trouble later, because a resolver that changes its own address is a resolver that breaks every client that points at it. With the image written, I put the card into the Pi, connected it by cable rather than by wireless so the resolver never depends on the wireless link, and let it boot.

The install itself is short. I ran the installer, chose the upstream resolver defaults, and set an admin password I keep in the password manager. Then I opened the admin page in a browser and spent ten minutes learning where things are. The dashboard shows the queries of the last twenty-four hours, which clients asked, and which ones got blocked, and that view has been the most useful part of the whole thing.

The blocklists are where the work is. The default list is small, so I added a handful of well-maintained community lists and let them build. Together they total about 1.2 million domains, which is far more than I expected, and the block rate settled around a fifth of all queries. I check the list count whenever I add a list, so a list that grows strangely stands out.

Then I handed DHCP over from the router to the Pi. That is the step that makes the whole system work properly, because the Pi can then tell every client which resolver to use on the next lease. I shortened the lease time for a week so the change took effect quickly, then set it back. Clients now point at the Pi as their only resolver, which is deliberate. If I left a public resolver in the client settings as a second option, some devices would quietly use it and bypass the filtering entirely.

The last pieces are the routines. Gravity runs weekly and rebuilds the blocklists from source, and I read the result when it finishes. The fallback resolver is a second upstream configured on the Pi, so if the forwarding target stops answering the Pi can still resolve through it, and I have a second Pi on the shelf that can take over the address if the first ever dies outright. I test that spare twice a year by booting it with the card out of the main Pi, so I know the image is still good and the settings still match. A spare that has never been booted is a spare I do not trust.

The order I did things in mattered more than the individual settings. I flashed the card, gave the Pi a static lease, and only then pointed anything at it. If I had pointed the clients at the Pi first, the whole house would have gone dark the moment I made a mistake, and I would have been fixing it with no working resolver to look things up with. Doing the lease first meant that when I did make a mistake in the blocklists, only my own test device went quiet, and I could undo it calmly from a machine that still knew how to reach the internet.

I keep a short written note of the whole build in my documentation repository, with the blocklist sources, the lease details, and the forwarding settings, so a rebuild is a copy of that note and a fresh flash rather than an archaeology project. The note also records why each choice was made, because the reason for a choice is the part I forget first, and a set of settings without reasons is a set of settings I will change by accident. The blocklists themselves are the least stable part of the whole build, because a source can go quiet or start over-blocking, so I review the sources once a quarter and drop any that have stopped being maintained. A dead source is worse than no source, because it looks like protection while quietly doing nothing. I also keep the query log retention modest, so the card is not filled by history I rarely read, and I read the log on the Pi rather than shipping it anywhere else, since the log is a map of everything the house does and I would rather it stayed at home.


Unbound runs on the Pi as well, and that is the part I am happiest with in the end. Unbound is a small validating resolver that sits in front of the upstream, and I have it forwarding to Quad9 over TLS on port 853, so the queries leave my house encrypted and are validated on the way back. It took an evening to configure and it is the reason I would not go back to asking a plain public server. The forwarding is deliberately narrow; I point it at Quad9 and nothing else, so I always know where my queries go.


## Maintenance

The weekly gravity update is the main routine, and it takes a couple of minutes. I read the summary and confirm the list count is in the region I expect. I watch the query log most weeks, not for anything in particular, but because it is where I notice a device phoning home or a name that keeps getting blocked for someone in the house. Disk space on the card matters more than people expect, because the query database grows with traffic, and I trim it when the card gets past half full. Once a month I take a teleporter backup, which packs the settings and the lists into one file I copy off the Pi. If the card dies, that file plus a fresh flash is a twenty-minute rebuild. I have never needed that file for real, but I have used it once to move the settings to the spare Pi while I replaced the main card, and it turned an evening into a quarter of an hour. I also keep the firmware on the card up to date once a quarter, when the gravity update is quiet, and I read the release notes before I do, because a resolver that reboots into a problem is a whole house with no names.

## Troubleshooting

Clients that ignore the Pi are almost always holding an old lease, so I renew the lease on the device or wait for it to expire. One device that stops resolving while everything else is fine is usually the device's own settings, and it is worth checking whether it has a hard-coded resolver that bypasses mine. The container losing its address is the other case, and it happens when it boots before the network is ready, so I check whether it picked the address the lease reserved or gave itself something else. A restart of the service normally returns it to the right address, and the static lease is what keeps it there. A block that someone in the house needs, usually a shopping or a delivery site, shows up as a client complaint rather than a fault, and the fix is a whitelist entry on the admin page rather than a change to the lists. I keep the whitelist short and reviewed, because a whitelist that grows every week quietly undoes the filtering I set the whole thing up for. If several devices stop resolving at once I check the Pi first, then the fallback, and only then the router, since the router is the thing least likely to have changed and the most annoying to reset.
